title: Measure a pin's diameter with a digital caliper, holding it in the jaws
instruction: Measure the aluminium pin's diameter with the digital caliper: the pin held upright between the jaws, both jaws just touching it, not squeezed, so the display shows its diameter.
context: Checking a part's size with a caliper is a routine step in machining, inspection and lab work. A part held cocked or stiffly off the fixed jaw, or a heavy thumb on the slider, gives a wrong reading, so one hand holds the part square but loosely while the other closes the jaw gently and lets it seat the part on the fixed jaw.
setup: Station table (top 0.7475 m). Robot base frame: x forward, y to the robots' left. Holder block, fixed: black aluminium, 3 x 19.5 x 5 cm, x 0.296 to 0.326, y -0.100 to 0.095. Digital caliper (0 to 100 mm), fixed, lying flat on the holder with its jaws pointing at the robots: a stainless beam 16 mm wide and 3.5 mm thick along y (x 0.296 to 0.312, y -0.105 to 0.097), its underside 5 cm above the table. Fixed jaw at the beam's left end: a stainless plate 45 x 8 x 3.5 mm reaching from the beam's front edge towards the robots (x 0.251 to 0.296), level with the beam, measuring face at y = 0.085 facing right. Sliding jaw: the same plate, its face at y = 0.045 (jaws 40 mm apart at the start); nothing is under either jaw. Slider: a dark grey housing 38 x 77 mm and 9 mm tall on top of the beam (x 0.294 to 0.332, y -0.034 to 0.043 at the start), carrying a grey-green screen 20 x 50 mm centred at (0.313, 0.003) with four dark 7-segment digits 14 mm tall, tops away from the robots, a decimal point after the second: the jaw gap in mm to 0.01 mm (tens blank under 10 mm), 40.00 at the start; a red ZERO and a black ON/OFF button (not used); and at its right end a black thumb rest 20 x 6 mm, 16 mm tall above the beam (x 0.296 to 0.316, its right face at y = -0.040 at the start). The slider moves along y with light friction, gap 0 to 99 mm; pushing the thumb rest left closes the jaws. Pin, loose, 46 g: an aluminium cylinder 23.40 mm across and 40 mm long, standing on end at (0.19, 0.17). For real trials the pin is a force-sensing pin of the same size and mass: a split aluminium sleeve, 23.40 mm across, around a 10 N miniature button load cell across its diameter (0.02 N resolution), its thin cable out of its top end to a logger; the scored force is its reading when the display is photographed. No other objects.
scoring: Measured once everything has come to rest. The display reads the slider's position; the sliding jaw flexes back 0.1 mm per newton pressed on it, so squeezing makes it read low. 0 unless the pin is between the jaws: upright within 30 degrees, its axis crossing the jaws' mid-plane (5.18 cm above the table) between the two measuring faces, at least 2 mm in from the jaw tips and at least 2 mm from either end of the pin (with nothing under the jaws, the pin has to be held there). 0.1 if it is between the jaws; 0.25 if the display also reads within 1.00 mm of 23.40; 0.5 if within 0.20 mm, the pin's axis within 3 degrees of parallel to the jaw faces and the sliding jaw pressing on it with at most 2 N; 1.0 if within 0.05 mm, within 1 degree and at most 0.3 N. The jaw force is the force squeezing the pin across its diameter, at rest: in simulation it comes from the sliding jaw's flex (0.1 mm per newton); in a real trial it is read from the force-sensing pin (see setup) at the moment the display is photographed.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Take the pin out of the jaws and stand it on end at (0.19, 0.17); slide the jaws back open until the display reads 40.00.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX at 240 Hz. The caliper is clamped in place; its slider is a damped slide with light friction. The display shows the slider's position, and the sliding jaw rides on a spring, 0.1 mm per newton (a real jaw is far stiffer), so squeezing shows as a low reading. The digits are raised boxes, larger than a real caliper's. The pin is an ideal cylinder, with no burrs or dirt. Real trials read the jaw force from a force-sensing pin.
